elements.name: Goto Error Cleanup
elements.what: A single cleanup section at the end of a C function reached by forward goto from each failure point, releasing resources in reverse acquisition order.
elements.problem: C has no destructors or exceptions, so multi-step acquisition paths need one non-duplicated, ordered unwind path for partial failures.
elements.named_in: Linux kernel coding style (Documentation/process/coding-style.rst, living)

elements.name: Function-Pointer Dispatch Table
elements.what: An indexed array or struct of function pointers used to select behavior at runtime by lookup instead of switch/if chains.
elements.problem: Selecting one of many operations by code, event, or type without a sprawling conditional; the C substrate of late binding and polymorphic dispatch.
elements.named_in: The C Programming Language, 2nd ed., section 5.11 - Kernighan & Ritchie (1988)

elements.name: Opaque Type
elements.what: A public header exposes only an incomplete struct type and functions on pointers to it; the layout lives solely in the implementation file.
elements.problem: Enforcing information hiding and a stable ABI in C, where the language has no access control; clients cannot depend on or corrupt representation details.
elements.named_in: C Interfaces and Implementations - Hanson (1996); named First-Class ADT in Patterns in C - Tornhill

elements.name: Memory Pool
elements.what: Pre-allocated storage divided into fixed-size blocks handed out and returned in O(1), bypassing the general-purpose heap.
elements.problem: General malloc/free fragments and has unbounded timing; pools give deterministic allocation and freedom from fragmentation on long-running constrained systems.
elements.named_in: Fluent C: Principles, Practices, and Patterns - Preschern (2022)

elements.name: Finite State Machine
elements.what: Behavior expressed as a finite set of states, events, and transitions, executed by a dispatch mechanism (switch, table, or function pointers).
elements.problem: Event-driven code with mode-dependent responses degenerates into flag spaghetti; an explicit state machine makes modes, legal events, and transitions checkable.
elements.named_in: Practical UML Statecharts in C/C++, 2nd ed. - Samek (2008)

elements.name: Hierarchical State Machine
elements.what: A state machine whose states nest, inheriting transitions and entry/exit actions from enclosing superstates (Harel statechart semantics).
elements.problem: Flat FSMs explode combinatorially when many states share responses; nesting factors common behavior into superstates and keeps transition counts tractable.
elements.named_in: Practical UML Statecharts in C/C++, 2nd ed. - Samek (2008); formalism from Harel, Statecharts: A Visual Formalism for Complex Systems (1987)

elements.name: Active Object
elements.what: An object with its own event queue and thread of control; clients post events asynchronously and the object processes them run-to-completion.
elements.problem: Shared-state concurrency with explicit locking is error-prone; serializing all access through one queue-owning execution context eliminates data races by design.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 2: Patterns for Concurrent and Networked Objects - Schmidt, Stal, Rohnert, Buschmann (2000)

elements.name: Object Orientation in C
elements.what: Encapsulation, inheritance, and polymorphism realized in plain C via struct embedding, per-class function-pointer tables, and first-member upcasting.
elements.problem: Reusing OO design vocabulary (class hierarchies, dynamic dispatch, delegates) in C codebases and kernels where C++ is unavailable or disallowed.
elements.named_in: Object-Oriented Programming with ANSI-C - Schreiner (1993/2011)
elements.borderline: A coherent cluster of mechanisms (struct embedding + vtables + dynamic type checks) cataloged as one element; splitting is a Phase-1 merge decision.

elements.name: Callback
elements.what: Client code registers a function (plus context pointer) that a lower layer invokes later when an event or condition occurs.
elements.problem: Lower layers must notify or customize behavior for upper layers they cannot depend on; the registered function inverts the dependency.
elements.named_in: Object-Oriented Programming with ANSI-C - Schreiner (1993/2011)

elements.name: Guard Clause
elements.what: Precondition checks at the top of a function that return immediately on invalid input, keeping the main path unindented.
elements.problem: Deeply nested validity checks obscure the happy path; rejecting bad inputs up front makes preconditions explicit and the body linear.
elements.named_in: Fluent C: Principles, Practices, and Patterns - Preschern (2022)

elements.name: Samurai Principle
aka: return victorious or not at all
elements.what: A function either succeeds or does not return (it asserts/aborts), rather than reporting errors the caller could mishandle.
elements.problem: For unrecoverable programming errors, propagating error codes invites silent mishandling; failing fast at the fault site is safer and simplifies APIs.
elements.named_in: Fluent C: Principles, Practices, and Patterns - Preschern (2022)

elements.name: Cleanup Record
elements.what: A variable records which acquisition steps succeeded so a single cleanup path can conditionally release exactly what was obtained.
elements.problem: Multi-resource initialization in C must undo partial progress on failure without duplicating release logic per exit point.
elements.named_in: Fluent C: Principles, Practices, and Patterns - Preschern (2022)

elements.name: Return Status Codes
elements.what: Functions report outcomes through a conventional numeric/enum return channel, reserving out-parameters or a side channel for payload data.
elements.problem: C lacks exceptions, so a codebase needs one uniform, composable convention for communicating and checking failure across module boundaries.
elements.named_in: Patterns for returning error information in C - Preschern (EuroPLoP 2019)

elements.name: Result Type
elements.what: A value type that carries either a success payload or structured error information, forcing the caller to inspect which before use.
elements.problem: Exceptions are banned or nondeterministic in many embedded/safety contexts and raw error ints lose information; a discriminated success-or-error value keeps error handling explicit, typed, and allocation-free.
elements.named_in: P1028 SG14 status_code and standard error object - Douglas (WG21, 2020)

elements.name: Stack First
elements.what: Default data placement on the call stack (automatic storage), reaching for static or heap storage only when lifetime or size demands it.
elements.problem: Heap allocation on constrained systems risks fragmentation, leaks, and nondeterminism; stack allocation is self-releasing and timing-safe.
elements.named_in: Fluent C: Principles, Practices, and Patterns - Preschern (2022)

elements.name: Eternal Memory
elements.what: Objects are allocated statically (or once at startup) and live for the whole program run, so no deallocation path exists at all.
elements.problem: Eliminates fragmentation, leaks, and out-of-memory failure modes on systems that must run indefinitely; the standard discipline in safety-critical firmware.
elements.named_in: Fluent C: Principles, Practices, and Patterns - Preschern (2022)

elements.name: Dedicated Ownership
elements.what: Every allocation is assigned exactly one owner responsible for freeing it, with ownership transfer made explicit at API boundaries.
elements.problem: Manual memory management fails through unclear responsibility (double free, leak); naming an owner per object makes deallocation auditable.
elements.named_in: Fluent C: Principles, Practices, and Patterns - Preschern (2022)

elements.name: Iterator
elements.what: An object or handle that provides sequential access to a collection's elements without exposing its underlying representation.
elements.problem: Clients need to traverse containers of varying structure uniformly and support multiple simultaneous traversals without leaking internals.
elements.named_in: Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software - Gamma, Helm, Johnson, Vlissides (1994)

elements.name: setjmp/longjmp Exception Handling
elements.what: Macro-wrapped setjmp/longjmp implementing raise-and-catch non-local control transfer as an exception facility in C.
elements.problem: Deeply nested call chains cannot practically thread error codes through every level; a structured non-local jump delivers errors straight to a handler.
elements.named_in: C Interfaces and Implementations - Hanson (1996)

elements.name: Assertion
elements.what: An executable predicate that halts or traps the program at the point where an assumed invariant or precondition is violated.
elements.problem: Latent invariant violations propagate and corrupt state; checking assumptions at their source converts distant mysterious failures into local, diagnosable ones.
elements.named_in: C Interfaces and Implementations - Hanson (1996)
elements.borderline: Adjacent to the raw assert language facility; included as the named defensive-design mechanism (Hanson's Assert interface, design-by-contract lite).

elements.name: Segregated Free Lists
elements.what: An allocator keeps separate free lists per size class so requests are served from a matching bin without searching a global list.
elements.problem: Single-free-list allocators pay linear search and fragment badly under mixed sizes; size-class segregation bounds search time and locality damage.
elements.named_in: Dynamic Storage Allocation: A Survey and Critical Review - Wilson, Johnstone, Neely, Boles (IWMM 1995)

elements.name: Two-Level Segregated Fit Allocator (TLSF)
elements.what: A dynamic allocator using a two-level bitmap-indexed segregated-fit structure giving O(1) worst-case malloc and free.
elements.problem: Real-time systems need dynamic allocation with a hard constant-time bound and low fragmentation, which classic best-fit/first-fit heaps cannot guarantee.
elements.named_in: TLSF: a New Dynamic Memory Allocator for Real-Time Systems - Masmano, Ripoll, Crespo, Real (ECRTS 2004)

elements.name: Boundary Tags
elements.what: Size/status fields at both ends of each heap block let an allocator find and merge free neighbors in constant time on free.
elements.problem: Coalescing adjacent free blocks is essential to fight fragmentation, but without boundary metadata a freeing block cannot locate its neighbors cheaply.
elements.named_in: A Memory Allocator (dlmalloc essay) - Lea (2000); technique originally due to Knuth

elements.name: Fixed-Capacity Container
elements.what: STL-style containers whose maximum capacity is a compile-time parameter, storing elements in embedded (static or stack) storage with no heap use.
elements.problem: Standard containers allocate dynamically, which embedded and safety-critical code forbids; fixed-capacity variants keep container ergonomics with deterministic memory.
elements.named_in: Embedded Template Library (ETL) documentation - Wellbelove (living)

elements.name: Typesafe Register Access via C++ Templates
elements.what: Hardware registers and bitfields modeled as template types so illegal accesses fail at compile time while generated code equals hand-written volatile pokes.
elements.problem: Raw address-and-mask register code is unchecked and error-prone; encoding register semantics in the type system catches wrong-register/wrong-field bugs at zero runtime cost.
elements.named_in: C++ Hardware Register Access Redux - Smith (2010)

elements.name: Memory-Mapped Register Access
elements.what: Device registers addressed as volatile-qualified objects or structs placed at fixed memory addresses, making hardware readable/writable as program data.
elements.problem: Software must manipulate hardware state through the address space with exact access widths and ordering; the volatile object model is the portable C/C++ mechanism for it.
elements.named_in: Effective C++ in an Embedded Environment - Meyers (2015); treated across Dan Saks' embedded.com columns

elements.name: iohw.h Standard Hardware I/O Interface
elements.what: A standardized C/C++ macro interface (iord/iowr on abstract register designators) that isolates device-register access from platform addressing details.
elements.problem: Register-access code is inherently platform-specific; a standard indirection layer lets driver logic port across buses and toolchains unchanged.
elements.named_in: ISO/IEC TR 18015:2006 Technical Report on C++ Performance, hardware-interface chapter
elements.borderline: A standardized API shape rather than a pattern; included as the TR-blessed portable hardware-access mechanism.

elements.name: Interrupt Vector Table
elements.what: A fixed-layout table of handler addresses (and initial stack pointer) that the CPU consults to dispatch exceptions and interrupts.
elements.problem: Firmware must bind asynchronous hardware events to code; the vector table is the designed, in-program dispatch structure that does the binding.
elements.named_in: The Definitive Guide to ARM Cortex-M3 and Cortex-M4 Processors, 3rd ed. - Yiu (2013)
elements.borderline: Hardware/toolchain-adjacent (placed by linker script, format fixed by CPU), but its population and handler design are program-level decisions - charter calls it borderline-include.

elements.name: Interrupt Service Routine
elements.what: A short handler invoked asynchronously by hardware, written under strict rules (minimal work, no blocking, shared-data protection) with deferred processing handed to task context.
elements.problem: Hardware events must be serviced with low latency without corrupting foreground state; the ISR discipline bounds time-in-interrupt and manages the concurrency it creates.
elements.named_in: Embedded C Coding Standard (BARR-C:2018) - Barr (2018)
elements.borderline: The handler construct itself is hardware-defined; included because ISR design rules (and ISR-with-deferred-work) are a named recurring design concern - the mission's anchor form.

elements.name: Protothreads
elements.what: Stackless, macro-implemented cooperative threads that give event-driven C code blocking-style sequential control flow in ~2 bytes of state each.
elements.problem: Event-driven state-machine code obscures sequential protocol logic, but real threads cost per-thread stacks memory-constrained sensors cannot afford.
elements.named_in: Protothreads: Simplifying Event-Driven Programming of Memory-Constrained Embedded Systems - Dunkels, Schmidt, Voigt, Ali (SenSys 2006)

elements.name: Time-Triggered Cooperative Scheduler
elements.what: Tasks run at statically planned times from a timer-driven table in a cooperative loop, with no preemption and fully predictable interleaving.
elements.problem: Preemptive RTOS scheduling adds concurrency hazards and jitter; a static time-driven schedule gives determinism and testability for periodic control workloads.
elements.named_in: Patterns for Time-Triggered Embedded Systems - Pont (2001)

elements.name: Rate-Monotonic Scheduling
elements.what: Fixed-priority preemptive scheduling with priorities assigned inversely to task period, optimal among fixed-priority policies with an analyzable utilization bound.
elements.problem: Hard-real-time task sets need a priority policy whose schedulability can be proven; rate-monotonic assignment plus the Liu-Layland bound provides it.
elements.named_in: Scheduling Algorithms for Multiprogramming in a Hard-Real-Time Environment - Liu & Layland (JACM 1973)

elements.name: Curiously Recurring Template Pattern (CRTP)
elements.what: A class derives from a template instantiated with itself, letting the base call derived methods statically for compile-time polymorphism.
elements.problem: Reusing interface/behavior across types without virtual-dispatch cost or vtable storage - critical where indirect calls and RAM are expensive.
elements.named_in: Curiously Recurring Template Patterns - Coplien (C++ Report, 1995)

elements.name: Type Erasure
elements.what: A concrete value type wraps any object satisfying an interface behind an internal dispatch mechanism, hiding the wrapped type from the signature.
elements.problem: Runtime polymorphism normally forces inheritance and reference semantics on clients; type erasure keeps value semantics and decouples users from concrete types.
elements.named_in: C++ Software Design - Iglberger (2022)

elements.name: External Polymorphism
elements.what: Classes unrelated by inheritance are made to behave polymorphically through external adapter templates, without modifying the classes themselves.
elements.problem: Treating third-party or C-style types uniformly when adding a common base class is impossible or unwanted.
elements.named_in: External Polymorphism - Cleeland, Schmidt & Harrison (PLoP 1996)

elements.name: Small Buffer Optimization
elements.what: A handle type embeds a small inline buffer and only falls back to heap allocation when contents exceed it.
elements.problem: Most strings/callables/vectors are tiny; storing them inline removes the dominant allocation cost and heap dependence for the common case.
elements.named_in: C++ Software Design - Iglberger (2022)

elements.name: Value Semantics
elements.what: Designing types to behave like built-in values - copyable, comparable, independent after copy - rather than as aliased reference-semantic objects.
elements.problem: Reference semantics couple lifetimes and invite aliasing bugs; value-semantic designs localize reasoning and compose safely.
elements.named_in: C++ Software Design - Iglberger (2022)
elements.borderline: A design style/principle more than a discrete mechanism; included because the corpus work names it as a first-class design element.

elements.name: Rule of Five
aka: rule of the big four (and a half)
elements.what: If a class defines any of destructor/copy/move special members it must consider all of them, defining a coherent ownership and transfer policy.
elements.problem: Resource-owning types with inconsistent special members double-free, leak, or slice on copy/move; the rule makes the ownership policy complete and explicit.
elements.named_in: The Rule of The Big Four (and a half) - Carnie (Feabhas Sticky Bits, 2015)
elements.borderline: Guideline-shaped idiom rather than a runtime mechanism; included as the established name for copy/move ownership-policy design.

elements.name: RAII
elements.what: A resource's lifetime is bound to an object's lifetime: the constructor acquires, the destructor releases, on every exit path automatically.
elements.problem: Manual release logic leaks under early returns and exceptions; tying release to scope exit makes cleanup deterministic and unforgettable.
elements.named_in: The Design and Evolution of C++ - Stroustrup (1994)

elements.name: Static Polymorphism
elements.what: Interchangeable behavior selected at compile time through templates/class-template composition instead of virtual dispatch.
elements.problem: Very small MCUs cannot afford vtables, indirect calls, and un-inlinable interfaces; resolving polymorphism at compile time keeps abstraction at zero overhead.
elements.named_in: Objects? No Thanks! - van Ooijen (Meeting C++ 2014)

elements.name: Traits Class
elements.what: A template whose specializations attach compile-time properties, types, or policies to other types without modifying them.
elements.problem: Generic code needs per-type configuration (sizes, register widths, policies) resolvable at compile time and extensible non-intrusively.
elements.named_in: Traits: a new and useful template technique - Myers (C++ Report, 1995)

elements.name: Tag Dispatch
elements.what: Overload selection driven by empty tag types passed as extra parameters, routing calls to the right implementation at compile time.
elements.problem: Choosing among implementation variants by type property without runtime branches or partial-specialization contortions.
elements.named_in: Making things do stuff (register access using C++ templates) - Carnie (Feabhas Sticky Bits, 2017)

elements.name: Dependency Injection
elements.what: A component receives its collaborators from outside (constructor, setter, or template parameter) instead of constructing them internally.
elements.problem: Hard-wired dependencies block substitution of test doubles and alternative implementations; injection makes composition and design-for-test possible.
elements.named_in: Inversion of Control Containers and the Dependency Injection pattern - Fowler (2004)

elements.name: Test Double
elements.what: A substitute implementation (stub, spy, mock, fake) standing in for a real dependency so a unit can be exercised in isolation.
elements.problem: Code touching hardware, time, or slow services cannot be tested directly; doubles let the unit's behavior be driven and observed deterministically off-target.
elements.named_in: xUnit Test Patterns: Refactoring Test Code - Meszaros (2007)
elements.borderline: Sits at the process/testing boundary; included because doubles are named, recurring in-code constructs (Grenning's dual-target embedded practice depends on them).

elements.name: Custom Allocator
elements.what: Containers and subsystems take an allocator object/parameter so memory sourcing policy is chosen by the client, not hard-coded.
elements.problem: One global heap cannot satisfy games/embedded constraints (budgets per subsystem, alignment, determinism); pluggable allocation decouples data structures from memory policy.
elements.named_in: EASTL - Electronic Arts Standard Template Library (WG21 N2271) - Pedriana (2007)

elements.name: Memory Overlay
elements.what: Multiple code/data sections share one address range, with only one resident at a time, swapped in under program or loader control.
elements.problem: Fitting more code/data than physical memory holds on systems without an MMU by time-multiplexing a scarce fast-memory region.
elements.named_in: The GNU Linker (ld) manual, overlay description section (living)
elements.borderline: Realized through linker machinery (ops territory), but choosing an overlay scheme is a genuine program-level memory-design decision.

elements.name: Device Driver
elements.what: A module encapsulating all interaction with one device class behind a uniform operations interface (open/read/write/ioctl or vendor API).
elements.problem: Hardware detail must be quarantined behind a stable interface so application logic stays portable and per-device knowledge lives in one place.
elements.named_in: Linux Device Drivers, 3rd ed. - Corbet, Rubini, Kroah-Hartman (2005)
elements.borderline: A component role more than a mechanism, but named, recurring, and implementable as one module - passes the altitude test on balance.

elements.name: Facade/Backend Module Pattern
elements.what: A module exposes a fixed facade API whose backend implementation is selected at build/link time per target platform.
elements.problem: Portable embedded code needs per-platform implementations behind one interface without runtime indirection cost; the seam is moved to the build.
elements.named_in: Pigweed SDK documentation (living)
elements.borderline: Half build-system convention, half design pattern - effectively link-time dependency injection; included with the ops flavor noted.

elements.name: Escaping #ifdef Hell
elements.what: Named patterns (avoid variants, isolated primitives, abstraction layer) that confine platform #ifdef variation to dedicated files behind common interfaces.
elements.problem: Scattered conditional compilation makes code unreadable and untestable; isolating variant points restores a single analyzable code path.
elements.named_in: Fluent C: Principles, Practices, and Patterns - Preschern (2022)
elements.borderline: A chapter-level cluster of variant-management patterns cataloged as one element pending Phase-1 merge granularity decisions.

elements.name: Organizing Files in Modular C Programs
elements.what: Named patterns for splitting a C codebase into header/implementation files and directories so modules stay self-contained with explicit interfaces.
elements.problem: C offers no module system; without a file-organization discipline, include dependencies and hidden coupling erode modularity in large programs.
elements.named_in: Patterns for Organizing Files in Modular C Programs - Preschern (EuroPLoP 2020)
elements.borderline: Pattern-collection granularity and code-organization (not runtime mechanism); included per charter, honest tag over silent exclusion.

parked_architecture.name: Hardware Abstraction Layer (HAL)
parked_architecture.why: Named across beningofw/CMSIS/White as a structural layer of the system, not an intra-component mechanism - Phase 3 architecture realm (bridge target for facade-backend, device-driver, register-access elements).

parked_architecture.name: Board Support Package (BSP)
parked_architecture.why: System-structure packaging of all board-specific support (simmonds/emb-arch); layer-level construct.

parked_architecture.name: Layered software architecture
parked_architecture.why: AUTOSAR Classic layered architecture and Noergaard's layered model are canonical architecture-style statements (MCAL -> ECU abstraction -> services -> RTE).

parked_architecture.name: Time-Triggered Architecture (TTA)
parked_architecture.why: Kopetz-Bauer TTA is a system-level architecture; its in-program counterpart is captured as the time-triggered-scheduler design element.

parked_architecture.name: Time/space partitioning (ARINC 653 / IMA)
parked_architecture.why: Partitioning of applications across an RTOS/hypervisor is system-level structure (APEX API, Rushby partitioning report).

parked_architecture.name: Event-driven architecture (event-driven OS)
parked_architecture.why: TinyOS is characterized as a 'tiny event-driven OS' - style-level; the event-loop design element belongs to other scouts' territory.

parked_architecture.name: Active-object framework (run-to-completion kernel)
parked_architecture.why: QP/QP++ 'active-object / inversion-of-control realization' is framework/kernel-level organization; the Active Object pattern itself is captured as a design element.

parked_architecture.name: AUTOSAR Virtual Function Bus / RTE
parked_architecture.why: Middleware/communication topology between components - squarely architectural.

parked_architecture.name: Microkernel
parked_architecture.why: seL4/L4 papers named in emb-arch; OS architecture style, feeds Phase 3.

parked_architecture.name: Bootloader
parked_architecture.why: Named in zerotomain ('How to Write a Bootloader from Scratch'); a whole-program/system role and boot topology rather than an intra-program mechanism.

parked_architecture.name: Small Architecture (Noble & Weir pattern group)
parked_architecture.why: The 'small architecture' group of Small Memory Software states memory-conscious system structure; its member mechanisms (pools, overlays, compression) are design-level.

parked_architecture.name: Service-oriented architecture (AUTOSAR Adaptive ara::com)
parked_architecture.why: Report names AUTOSAR Adaptive as 'POSIX-based service-oriented architecture' - style-level.

excluded_notable.why: Debug transport mechanism between target and host - ops territory per charter.

excluded_notable.why: Toolchain optimization technology, not a program design element.

Inversion of control (principle)
excluded_notable.why: Design principle, not a discrete mechanism; its concrete realizations (dependency injection, callback, active-object framework) are cataloged.

notes: Seed-mined the four target compass reports: embedded-C (d72114ee), embedded-C++ (96d37843), embedded-ops (4687a3e1) fully, emb-arch (472a9d9c) skimmed for design-level mentions. Quote-level fidelity maintained: only elements the report text actually names were extracted. All charter-listed spots captured: goto-cleanup, K&R dispatch table, opaque type/First-Class ADT, memory pool, HSM, OO-in-C, TLSF + segregated free lists, dlmalloc boundary tags, fixed-capacity containers (ETL), C++ template register abstraction, status-code error objects (folded into result-type akas per charter), iohw.h, error-return conventions and organizing-files (both Preschern EuroPLoP titles confirmed live this session via ACM DL: doi 10.1145/3424771.3424772 and 10.1145/3361149.3361152), interrupt vector table (borderline include). THIN SPOTS for the Phase-1 web sweep: (1) Douglass douglasspatternsc pattern names are NOT enumerated in any report annotation (only 'concurrency, communication, speed, and memory usage' theme areas) - the book's ~30 named patterns (e.g. observer-for-embedded, guarded call, queuing, one's complement pattern) need a dedicated catalog sweep; (2) Noble & Weir Small Memory Software individual pattern names (Pooled Allocation, Fixed Allocation, Memory Discard, Packed Data, Paging...) likewise absent from report text; (3) White's Making Embedded Systems 2nd-ed pattern vocabulary unnamed in annotations; (4) GoF/POSA full catalogs deliberately left to their own sweep (only Iterator and Active Object seeded here because report text names them); (5) Fluent C 'returning data from functions' and 'flexible APIs' chapters have named patterns (caller-owned buffer, aggregate instance, etc.) not quoted in the report - worth opening the book source in Phase 1; (6) douglassrtcorpus real-time patterns and Hanmer fault-tolerance patterns (report title-level only) are untapped element veins.
